strengths: Clearly motivated and well-formalized problem: the paper defines a novel and practically relevant setting (pay-to-unlock feature licensing for LLMs) with a crisp set of requirements (R1-R4) that provide a useful lens for comparing prior password-locking work.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation: experiments span three base models (DeepSeek-Math, DeepSeek-Coder, Llama-3-8B-Instruct), four feature datasets, and multiple attack types (many-shot, GCG, TAP, AutoDAN-Turbo), including single- and multi-feature locking scenarios up to four simultaneous features.

The proposed spectral-norm-clipping merging strategy (Algorithm 1) is a simple, practically motivated fix to the observed 'over-refusal' failure mode when naively merging multiple refusal-trained adapters, and the paper shows a clear ablation against CAT/TIES/Linear merging baselines to justify it.

Direct, apples-to-apples comparisons with a password-locking baseline (PWD) on effectiveness, utility, robustness, and scalability provide reasonably convincing evidence that LOCKET dominates the baseline on the tested settings.
The paper is transparent about limitations (feature interference, limited number of features tested, model coverage, computation overhead) and promises code release, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is incremental: the method largely combines existing components (LAT from Sheshadri et al. 2025, CAT merging from Prabhakar et al. 2025, and a spectral-norm rescaling idea closely related to prior model-merging interference-reduction work such as STAR, which is only cited as a limitations reference rather than compared against empirically).

The hyperparameter τ for adapter clipping is tuned using samples drawn directly from each task's test set ("a random sample of 100 examples from each test set"), which raises concerns about test-set leakage/overfitting in the reported utility and effectiveness numbers, undermining confidence in the headline results.

The robustness metric (attack success rate via refusal-keyword matching) is coarse: it does not verify whether a 'successful' evasion actually elicits a correct/useful answer to the locked feature, nor guard against false positives/negatives from keyword-based classification of open-ended generations.

The adversary/threat model explicitly excludes fine-tuning-based attacks by assuming black-box deployment, but many commercial LLM providers (including OpenAI) offer fine-tuning APIs, so this exclusion may understate real-world attack surface; the paper does not address decomposition/multi-turn attacks that could reconstruct locked feature outputs from combinations of authorized queries.

Observed feature interference (e.g., Math vs. MMLU, causing up to 7% utility drop or worse) suggests the approach is sensitive to feature overlap, which could be a significant practical limitation as the number of real-world features grows; scalability is only demonstrated up to 4 features, with claims beyond that resting on speculation from a different paper (Lee et al., 2025) rather than empirical validation.

Utility evaluation relies solely on automated metrics (accuracy, ROUGE-1) without human evaluation of response quality, which is particularly weak for open-ended tasks like summarization where ROUGE-1 alone can be a poor proxy for quality.

The motivating business case (pay-per-feature LLM monetization) is speculative and not empirically grounded beyond a single tweet citation, slightly weakening the broader significance argument, though the technical contribution (robust adapter-based access control) has merit independent of this framing.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper carefully enumerates requirements (effectiveness, utility-preservation, robustness, scalability) for a feature-locking technique (FLoTE) and uses this framework to systematically expose gaps in prior password-locking work (Greenblatt et al., Su et al., Tang et al.) as well as several strawman alternatives (system prompts, routing, detectors).

The core technical contribution -- clipping the spectral norm of merged LoRA adapters to curb 'over-refusal' reinforcement -- is simple, well-motivated by an observed failure mode (repeated 'sorry, sorry, sorry...' generations), and is empirically shown to outperform standard merging baselines (CAT, TIES, Linear/Task Arithmetic) on utility preservation (Figure 2, Top).

Fairly comprehensive empirical evaluation across 3 base models (DeepSeek-Math, DeepSeek-Coder, Llama-3-8B-Instruct), 4 feature domains, and multiple attack types (many-shot, GCG, TAP, AutoDAN-Turbo), with consistent, favorable comparisons to a reimplemented password-locking baseline (PWD) on effectiveness, utility, robustness, and multi-feature scalability.
Reasonable ablation on the merging hyperparameter τ, illustrating the effectiveness/utility trade-off and providing a principled tuning procedure.

The threat model (naive/non-adaptive/adaptive jailbreaks, credential sharing) is clearly specified and appropriately scoped to the black-box API setting, distinguishing the paper's contribution from white-box fine-tuning attacks that are out of scope.
weaknesses: The robustness (R3) evaluation relies on a keyword-based ASR metric (absence of words like 'sorry', 'I cannot', 'unable') to judge attack success. This is a weak and potentially gameable proxy: it does not verify that a 'successful' jailbreak actually elicits a correct/useful response for the locked feature, nor does it check whether refusals phrased differently are miscounted as successful attacks. No human or LLM-judge verification of attack outputs is reported, which undermines confidence in the R3 robustness numbers being interpreted as genuine capability leakage rather than surface-level keyword avoidance.

Scalability claims are only empirically validated up to 4 features and small combinations thereof; the paper explicitly defers evaluation with more features to future work and instead speculates about scaling to ~12 features by citing an unrelated paper (Lee et al., 2025), which weakens the 'scalable' claim relative to the strong framing in the abstract/title.

The per-feature-combination clipping threshold τ appears to require separate tuning for each new feature and combination, as shown by the large table of different τ values in Appendix B. This raises a concern about whether the practical scalability of the approach (a core selling point vs. prior work) is undermined by this manual/combinatorial tuning overhead, which is not discussed as a limitation.

The technical novelty is somewhat incremental: it combines existing components (Latent Adversarial Training from Sheshadri et al., 2025, and spectral-norm-based rescaling closely related to existing merging-interference literature such as TIES/CAT/Task-Singular-Vectors) rather than introducing fundamentally new machinery; the contribution is more in the problem framing and careful engineering/combination than a novel algorithmic idea.

The access control and client authentication mechanisms, central to the proposed pay-to-unlock system, are simply assumed ('we assume the service provider has ways of identifying and authenticating clients') rather than addressed, leaving a nontrivial part of the overall system model outside the technical contribution.

Two of the three base models (DeepSeek-Math, DeepSeek-Coder) are already narrowly specialized models, which may make locking their core specialty easier or behave differently than locking a feature in a general-purpose chat model; only one general-purpose model (Llama-3-8B-Instruct) is tested, limiting generalizability of the results.

The economic premise (pay-to-unlock schemes being more profitable, feature-level monetization) is asserted but not empirically or analytically substantiated beyond a single anecdotal tweet and a citation to mobile-game monetization; this framing motivates the paper but is not core to its technical validity.

strengths: Clear and well-organized problem formulation, with explicit requirements (effectiveness, utility-preservation, robustness, scalability) and a systematic comparison table showing how prior password-locking/backdoor techniques fail each requirement.

Technically interesting contribution: combining Latent Adversarial Training for robust refusal with a novel spectral-norm-clipping approach to LoRA adapter merging that explicitly targets the previously undocumented 'over-refusal' failure mode of standard merging methods (CAT/TIES/Linear).

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning three base models (DeepSeek-Math, DeepSeek-Coder, Llama-3-8B, plus a 70B scale check), four/eight feature combinations, and four attack types (many-shot, GCG, TAP, AutoDAN-Turbo), together with ablations against merging alternatives and against a strong PWD+CircuitBreaking baseline.

Reasonable attention to practical deployment concerns: runtime/storage overhead measurements, discussion of decoding-temperature variance, and appendices with hyperparameters and dataset splits that aid reproducibility.
Honest discussion of feature-interference and 'arms race' robustness limitations rather than overstating universality of the approach.
weaknesses: The economic motivation (pay-to-unlock premium LLM features via refusal-based locking) is thinly justified—supported mainly by a single tweet and unrelated SaaS/gaming citations—raising questions about whether this is a genuine, impactful use case for the NLP community versus a somewhat contrived framing for a model-editing/merging paper.

Apparent inconsistency between the described merging algorithm (Algorithm 1: a single offline, per-layer clipping threshold computed once from all adapters) and the appendix, which reports distinct tuned τ values for every different feature combination; if τ must be retuned per client-authorization subset, this reintroduces a scalability concern similar to the combinatorial-explosion critique the paper levels against routing/gateway baselines, undermining the R4 scalability claim.

Robustness evaluation uses generic, off-the-shelf jailbreak attacks (many-shot, GCG, TAP, AutoDAN) rather than adaptive attacks that specifically target the adapter-merging/spectral-clipping mechanism itself; the paper assumes (via transfer arguments from other work) that single-feature-locked robustness generalizes to merged multi-feature settings without directly validating this empirically.

The claim of resistance to credential sharing (R3.4) is asserted almost by definition (no password exists) but does not analyze other forms of authorization circumvention (e.g., session/token sharing, API key sharing at the account level), leaving this requirement only superficially addressed.

Utility degradation from feature interference (e.g., Math–MMLU, up to 7%, worse for overlapping MMLU subdomains in the 8-feature scalability experiment) is acknowledged but not deeply diagnosed or mitigated, and no human/qualitative evaluation of refusal message naturalness or detectability is provided.

Variance/robustness of results across random seeds is only checked in one narrow setting (Appendix F, single model/feature, 10 runs), leaving open questions about the stability of the many other reported numbers, especially attack success rates which can be sensitive to attack randomness.
